title: Latest Essay by Maksym Kryvosh (Plokhoi), Liberation Prisoner in Ukraine
content:
I was taken from my cell to a room to participate in a court hearing remotely, via video conference. The court was considering a petition from the prison guards to place me in solitary confinement for two months. (For the kleptocracy known as Ukraine, it wasn’t enough that I’ve been in solitary for seven years, or the 13-year sentence I was awarded for fighting for Justice; they also had to throw me into the punishment cell for periods ranging from 14 days to three months—bringing my total to 18 stints in the punishment cell over three years).

The judge was reading out the ruling, but I wasn’t listening anymore, nor was I looking at the monitor. I was looking at the window—a large moth was beating its wings against the glass. It was unclear how it had gotten there; the windows were sealed shut. I told the guards: I won’t go back to the cell until I set it free… It worked! Outside, I opened my palms; it was a Peacock butterfly—the most beautiful butterfly I had ever seen—its colors shimmering and mesmerizing in the sunlight. It felt at ease on my palm and didn’t want to fly away. For a whole minute, we were happy.

title: Lies the Fur Industry Tells!
content:
Mink and fox killers and their apologists often say the most ridiculous things to try and mitigate their losses after raids like the two we have seen in the last couple of months, in which 3000 or more captive mink were liberated from horrific captivity. Sample absurdities spouted as fact include:

Lie #1: Many or most of the escaped animals were run over and killed by cars.

– The absurdity of this statement is that before liberation, death was 100% certain. Every animal on the farm was bred to die by the end of November. While it is true a small number may be hit by cars after being released, most will not, and if nothing else they have been given a chance at freedom. In reality, fox and mink farms are located in rural areas with little traffic, the animals are quick and solitary animals, and it beggars belief to imagine them aggregating in the road waiting to be run over by the rare passing vehicle.

– Mink are in fact only a few generations removed from their wild cousins and have not yet had their wild instincts bred out. The “Mink Rehabilitation Project” led by convicted ALF liberator Rod Coronado proved this decades ago. title: Activists Release 1,500 Mink From Idaho Farm
content:
Activists called the raid on an Idaho mink farm “liberation” for the 1,500 minks they released. But they can’t take care of themselves, said the farm’s owner, leaving many to die of heat, stress or get run over. “This is an unethical thing to do,” he said.

Intent on liberating caged animals, masked protesters broke into a family-owned mink farm in southeast Idaho, less than 80 miles west of Wyoming, and released 1,500 mink into the wild on Saturday.

Farm owner Jeff Hobbs told Cowboy State Daily that instead of freedom, the activists delivered a death sentence, leaving the animals to perish from dehydration, stress, heat or getting run over on the road.

“This is an unethical thing to do to animals,” Hobbs said. “Regardless of your value system, I haven’t quite figured out how you can claim that you’re doing something for the benefit of the animals that’s so harmful to them.”

When he spoke to Cowboy State Daily on Tuesday, Hobbs said he was still working to gather the loose minks in Franklin County. At this point, he said about 90% of the mink have been caught but still face health risks from the trauma of being temporarily released.

“This stressed them hard,” Hobbs said. “You stress animals and you run into problems. You have to do something to offset that stress so this has created a serious herd health problem.”

Hobbs said the break-in happened around 2:30 a.m. Saturday. Mink were almost immediately killed by passing cars and several more were running around the area, Hobbs said.

“Immediately we started calling out to people that we thought could assist us, and word spread in the community,” Hobbs said. “In a short time, I had almost 100 people here help them to catch animals.”

In a Saturday statement, the Franklin County Sheriff’s Office said it was investigating the incident. The department did not respond to Cowboy State Daily by publication.

On Sunday, the North American Animal Liberation Press Office posted a statement celebrating the release of the mink.

“The animals liberated this weekend have a fighting chance at life,” the statement said. “They faced a 100 percent death rate if they stayed on the farm.”

In an email to Cowboy State Daily, North American Animal Liberation press officer Jerry Vlasak disputed claims from Hobbs and the sheriff’s office that most of the mink had been recaptured.

“Almost surely did not happen,” Vlasak said. “These mink are not domesticated as the farmers claim. Scientific studies have shown them to be easily able to survive in the wild when they are released.”

Challis Hobbs, Jeff Hobbs’ son and executive director of Fur Commission USA, said in a Saturday statement that the action should be handled as a federal offense under the Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act.

“Those responsible for this attack are terrorists, plain and simple,” Challis Hobbs said.

Vlasak threw that same label back at Challis Hobbs and the Fur Commission USA.

“Those who breed, imprison and kill thousands of innocent animals every year to make a profit are the real terrorists,” Vlasak said.

Hobbs said that his fourth-generation family farm has long been the target of animal-rights organizations. In the 1990s and early 2000s, Hobbs said, authorities warned him twice that his farm ranked high on a list of likely targets and recommended he increase security.

Since then, he said, drones have flown over the property and people have driven by with cameras. Hobbs said a drone flew over the farm on Oct. 6, his father’s birthday, and was seen by a family friend who was preparing for a party.

“She didn’t realize that was a threat until after the release,” Hobbs said.

Hobbs said he understands people have different values and are entitled to be against the business of harvesting mink for fur.

“But none of us are entitled to try to press our value system on other people,” Hobbs said.

Moreover, he said the action of releasing 1,500 minks, which have no skills to survive in the wild, is antithetical to the larger goal of animal welfare.

“When people come in and do something this blatant, it’s done a lot of damage,” Hobbs said. “Animals are dying because of it.”

He also said releasing 1,500 mink, which have no skills to survive in the wild, runs counter to the larger goal of animal welfare. For Vlasak, it’s “laughable” for Hobbs, who profits from harvesting and selling mink pellets, to claim concern for the animals.

“The mink are born in February or March and are killed by gassing, clubbing or anal electrocution in November, before being skinned, sometimes while still alive, for their fur,” Vlasak said.

While Hobbs claimed a similar timeline from birth to harvest, he said the nature of how the minks are killed is far from the truth.

“They’re euthanized with carbon monoxide,” Hobbs said. “They just go to sleep.”

Hobbs said the mink live healthy lives on the farm, with constant access to fresh water, a balanced daily diet and warm, dry nests. He said the farm also has a herd-health program to treat animals that get sick.

Susan Curtis, director of Sandy’s Haven, a wildlife rescue service in Preston, Idaho, told Cowboy State Daily the Hobbs Family Farm has a local reputation for farming fur as ethically as possible.

“I would absolutely love it if the mink farming went away forever but I know they’re doing it as humanely as possible,” Curtis said. “I’ve never had any issue with the Hobbses.”

What the activists did, Curtis said, took the mink from a “bad situation and put them in a worse situation.” The release also endangers local wildlife by dropping the mink back into an ecosystem where they can strain the food supply, Curtis said, and it puts domestic animals, including outdoor pets, at risk of attack.

Already, Curtis said she’s heard of one wild goose with bite marks and a resident whose dog was attacked by one of the newly freed mink.

“These are definitely carnivores and predators, these little mink guys,” Curtis said.

That’s something that area resident Deirdre Burgess has learned the hard way.

“I live on the edge of town and I have chickens,” Burgess told Cowboy State Daily. “Or, I had chickens. I had 15 hens and 1 rooster and they killed my rooster and 10 of my hens.”

Burgess said her small flock was more pets than livestock. To lose all at once, and to encounter such a bloody scene in her backyard, was heartbreaking, she said.

“It was so sad,” Burgess said. “And it was just gross.”

Like Curtis, Burgess said she doesn’t agree with the business of fur. But simply freeing the animals, she said, condemned them to an almost certain death, and let the rest of them loose to do more damage.

“Do I buy furs? No,” Burgess said. “But on the other side of that, I wouldn’t turn all of those animals loose. There’s a humane way to do it. Letting them starve or get run over is absolutely no way to fix it. It doesn’t help.”

In 2015, activist Joseph Buddenberg was indicted under the Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act and later served two years in federal prison for his role in a cross-country campaign that released nearly 6,000 mink, including an estimated 1,800 animals from a farm in Burley, Idaho.

Though he does not claim a role in the most recent action, Buddenberg told Cowboy State Daily in an email that the Hobbs raid was justified.

“The fur industry’s days are numbered,” Buddenberg said. “Compassionate activists will continue to open cages and shut these places down.”

Emma Jane Jackson can be reached at emma@cowboystatedaily.com.

content:

title: Dixon Mink Farm in Bluffdale, Utah will be Forced to Close
content:
Dixon Mink Farm at 15028 Pony Express Road in the town of Bluffdale, Utah will be forced to close.

The city council of Bluffdale has eliminated fur farming as a permitted use. Fur farms will be unable to operate in Bluffdale.

The councilperson who pushed for the change said:

“I saw the serious issue the mink farm had on the lives of our residents. As I knocked on doors of our independence area there were so many flies people couldn’t open their door to talk to me. Because of this ordinance change the city can not approve the business license for this or any other mink farm.”
